summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the summands indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) with opposite signs, forcing both sequences to vanish modulo \(p\) on \(p\le n\le2p-2\); at \(n=p-1\) their values are respectively \(1\) and \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), with central-binomial divisibility leaving only the midpoint in the second evaluation. Reversing the Hankel matrix columns therefore makes it triangular with constant diagonal, and the reversal’s \((p-1)/2\) transpositions make the sign persist in the first case and cancel in the second.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2
                 \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\), or equivalently are identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first record the binomial congruences that will be used. If
\(N=pq+r\) and \(K=ps+t\), where \(0\le r,t<p\), then the one-digit form of Lucas's congruence is
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom rt\binom qs\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, in \(\mathbb F_p[x]\),
\[
(1+x)^N=(1+x)^{pq+r}\equiv (1+x^p)^q(1+x)^r.
\]
Comparing the coefficient of \(x^{ps+t}\) gives (1). In particular, for \(0\le r,k<p\),
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk, \qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+k}\equiv\binom rk. \tag{2}
\]
We will refer to these as the low-index and high-index congruences.

Two congruences for central binomial coefficients are also needed. First, if \(0\le k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), then
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0. \tag{3}
\]
To see this, write \(2k=p+(2k-p)\). Formula (1) gives a factor
\(\binom{2k-p}{k}\), and this is zero because \(2k-p<k\), the last inequality being equivalent to \(k<p\).

Second, for every \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{2(p+k)}{p+k}\equiv 2\binom{2k}{k}. \tag{4}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2k<p\), then the base-\(p\) decompositions are
\[
2(p+k)=2p+2k,\qquad p+k=p+k,
\]
so (1) gives
\[
\binom{2(p+k)}{p+k}
 \equiv \binom{2k}{k}\binom21
 =2\binom{2k}{k}.
\]
If \(2k\ge p\), the right-hand side is zero by (3). On the left, the low base-\(p\) digits of the numerator and denominator are respectively \(2k-p\) and \(k\); since \(2k-p<k\), Lucas's congruence makes the left-hand side zero as well. Thus (4) holds in both cases.

Finally, for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k. \tag{5}
\]
For example, this follows directly from
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}.
\]
Since \(k!\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), it may be cancelled, and the numerator is congruent to
\((-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)=(-1)^k k!\).

We next prove the crucial vanishing of both sequences in the interval from \(p\) through \(2p-2\).

Fix \(r\) with \(0\le r<p\). Consider first \(a(p+r)\). Split its defining sum into indices \(0\le k<p\) and indices \(k=p+u\), where \(0\le u\le r\). Within the first part, every term with \(r<k<p\) vanishes modulo \(p\), because by (2)
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk=0.
\]
It remains to pair, for each \(0\le k\le r\), the term indexed by \(k\) with the term indexed by \(p+k\). By (2), both relevant binomial coefficients are congruent to \(\binom rk\):
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk,
\qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+k}\equiv\binom rk.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+k}=-(-1)^k.
\]
The two fourth powers are equal modulo \(p\), while their signs are opposite. Hence each pair cancels, and therefore
\[
a(p+r)\equiv0 \qquad(0\le r<p). \tag{6}
\]

The same pairing proves the corresponding assertion for \(c\), but we spell out the central-binomial factors. Again, terms with \(r<k<p\) vanish because \(\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk=0\). For \(0\le k\le r\), the term of \(c(p+r)\) indexed by \(k\) is
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^2
\binom{2k}{k}
\binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}.
\]
Here \(p+r-k=p+(r-k)\), so (2) and (4) show that this term is congruent to
\[
2(-1)^k\binom rk^2
\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}. \tag{7}
\]
The term indexed by \(p+k\) is
\[
(-1)^{p+k}\binom{p+r}{p+k}^2
\binom{2(p+k)}{p+k}
\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}.
\]
By (2), (4), and the oddness of \(p\), this is congruent to the negative of (7). Thus all remaining terms cancel in pairs, and
\[
c(p+r)\equiv0 \qquad(0\le r<p). \tag{8}
\]
In particular, both (6) and (8) apply throughout the interval
\(p\le n\le2p-2\), by writing \(n=p+r\) with \(0\le r\le p-2\).

We also need the values immediately preceding that vanishing interval. From (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are an odd number \(p\) of terms in this alternating sum, so adjacent \(1,-1\) pairs cancel and one final \(1\) remains. Therefore
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1. \tag{9}
\]

For \(c(p-1)\), recall that \(p-1=2m\). Its term indexed by \(k\) contains the two central binomial coefficients
\[
\binom{2k}{k}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}.
\]
If \(k>m\), then \(2k\ge p\), so the first one is zero modulo \(p\) by (3). If \(k<m\), then \(p-1-k>m\), and hence
\(2(p-1-k)\ge p\); the second one is zero modulo \(p\) by (3). Consequently every term vanishes except the middle term \(k=m\).

At this middle index, \(p-1-m=m\). Moreover, by (5),
\[
\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
Both the squared ordinary binomial factor and the product of the two central factors are therefore easy to evaluate:
\[
\binom{p-1}{m}^2\equiv1,
\qquad
\binom{2m}{m}^2
=\binom{p-1}{m}^2\equiv1.
\]
Thus the sole surviving term gives
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m. \tag{10}
\]

We now establish the determinant reduction that turns these sequence identities into the desired answer. Let \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb F_p\) be any function satisfying
\[
f(n)=0\quad\text{for }p\le n\le2p-2. \tag{11}
\]
Form the \(p\times p\) Hankel matrix
\[
M=(f(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reverse the order of its columns, and call the resulting matrix \(B\). Its \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
B_{ij}=f\bigl(i+(p-1-j)\bigr)=f(p-1+i-j).
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
p\le p-1+i-j\le2p-2,
\]
so (11) gives \(B_{ij}=0\). Hence \(B\) is upper triangular. Every diagonal entry is
\[
B_{ii}=f(p-1),
\]
and therefore
\[
\det B=f(p-1)^p. \tag{12}
\]

The reversal permutation on \(\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\) sends \(j\) to \(p-1-j\). Since \(p=2m+1\), it fixes the middle element \(m\) and consists otherwise of exactly \(m\) disjoint transpositions. Its sign is consequently \((-1)^m\). Reversing the columns therefore gives
\[
\det B=(-1)^m\det M. \tag{13}
\]
Since \(((-1)^m)^2=1\), equations (12) and (13) imply the general formula
\[
\det M=(-1)^m f(p-1)^p. \tag{14}
\]

Apply (14) first to the reduction of \(a(n)\) modulo \(p\). The required vanishing hypothesis is (6), and (9) gives \(f(p-1)=1\). Hence
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^m\cdot1^p
=(-1)^m
=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p. \tag{15}
\]

Next apply (14) to the reduction of \(c(n)\). The vanishing hypothesis is (8), while (10) gives \(f(p-1)=(-1)^m\). Therefore
\[
\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\equiv(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^m\). The last expression is thus
\[
(-1)^m(-1)^m=1. \tag{16}
\]

Finally, reducing an integer matrix modulo \(p\) commutes with taking its determinant, since the determinant is a sum of signed products of entries. Thus the determinant identities obtained in \(\mathbb F_p\) are precisely the asserted integer congruences (15) and (16). This proves both claims.
